overview: A two-page Department of State list of papers for decimal file 894.9111, “Newspaper clipping—Japan,” indexing items 4–21 rather than reproducing the underlying documents. The entries describe diplomatic submissions, press summaries, cartoons, clippings, Japanese news bulletins, and translations of Japanese-language newspapers from 1940 through 1944. Subjects include wartime portrayals of Franklin D. Roosevelt and Axis leaders, Japanese Embassy personnel in Washington, Japanese-language press monitoring by the Justice Department, propaganda distributed in Turkey, and extensive reporting on the Japanese press of Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers for file 894.9111
subfiles.about: This two-page index describes papers concerning Japanese newspapers, press translations, cartoons, clippings, and propaganda filed as items 4–21 under decimal file 894.9111.
subfiles.summary: Page 1 inventories items 4–10, including political cartoons transmitted from Japan, a summary of the Japanese press, police information about material dropped by Japanese Embassy attachés, and Justice Department summaries of the Japanese-language press. Page 2 continues with items 11–21, chiefly translations from Japanese newspapers published in Buenos Aires, along with information about a Pacific press service and Japanese news bulletins distributed in Turkey. Although the heading gives 1941–1942, the listed material ranges from December 1940 through at least May 1944. The underlying clippings, translations, memoranda, and diplomatic communications are described but are not reproduced in these pages.

interest: The index is useful for reconstructing the geographic reach of U.S. wartime monitoring of Japanese-language media, extending from Tokyo and Washington to Buenos Aires and Istanbul. Its descriptions preserve evidence about cartoons portraying Roosevelt and Axis leaders, police surveillance involving Japanese Embassy attachés immediately before Pearl Harbor, and the circulation of Japanese bulletins abroad. It also reveals an apparent archival inconsistency: a list headed “1941–1942” includes material dated from 1940 through 1944.
